title: Vermessene Philosophie
bookshelves: Category: Reference, Information and Interdisciplinary subjects
summary: In recent decades, scholarly publishing—including in philosophy—has shifted from print-based works to predominantly digital formats. But why should philosophers concern themselves with questions regarding university infrastructure? Why should representatives of the discipline think critically about electronic publishing processes? What do philosophers have to do with bibliometrics, and how does this alter philosophical work? The authors critically examine current electronic publishing practices and the quantitative assessment of scholarly expertise based upon them. In this context, philosophy functions both as a discipline that utilizes these systems and as a field dedicated to critical reflection: (1) As users of information and communication technologies (ICT), philosophers encounter—in their daily work—developments and challenges related to electronic publishing (e.g., funding for Article Processing Charges [APCs], repositories, new forms of scholarly communication via social media, Open Access, etc.) as well as the associated phenomenon of bibliometric performance assessment (e.g., Journal Impact Factor, h-index, etc.). (2) As experts in the critical reflection of processes of scientific inquiry, the epistemic division of labor, the interplay between science and society, and the attendant difficulties, they are also the ones who—through critical analysis—investigate questions concerning expertise, trust, autonomy, and scientific progress. In this volume, representatives of the discipline engage in a dialogue with experts from information and library sciences at both universities and non-university research institutions. The contributions address questions such as: How can the scholarly community assert its autonomy against an oligopoly of information analysts within the context of electronic publishing? How can troubling trends—such as the tracking of researchers—be reversed? What criteria and standards should the scientific community apply to its own assessment of expertise in the future?
